summary.text: A planetary nebula is an expanding, glowing shell of ionized gas that red giant stars eject late in their lives.
The name comes from their round, planet-like look in early telescopes, but they are unrelated to planets.
They form at the end of the life of a star of intermediate mass, the Sun is expected to form one, and they last perhaps a few tens of millennia.

facts.label: Star mass
facts.value: Form from stars of about 1 to 8 solar masses

facts.label: How long they last
facts.value: Perhaps a few tens of millennia

facts.label: First one found
facts.value: The Dumbbell Nebula, seen by Messier on July 12, 1764

facts.label: What lights them
facts.value: Ultraviolet radiation from the hot, exposed core

items.prompt: These glowing shells have nothing to do with planets. Why do astronomers call them 'planetary'?

options.label: They are found orbiting around giant stars
They looked round like planets in early telescopes
They are made from the leftovers of planets
They shine the way planets do

items.explain: The word describes their planet-like round shape seen through early telescopes; they are unrelated to planets.

items.prompt: The gas a red giant has shed is glowing brightly. What makes it shine?

options.label: Heat from the gas colliding with itself
Light bounced back from distant stars
Fusion happening in the gas shell itself
Ultraviolet light from the star's hot exposed core

items.explain: Once the atmosphere has dissipated, ultraviolet radiation from the hot core ionizes the ejected material, and absorbed ultraviolet light energizes the shell so it glows.

items.prompt: A star's life has phases lasting millions of years or longer. How does a planetary nebula compare?

options.label: It is short-lived, perhaps a few tens of millennia
It is the longest phase of the star's life
It lasts as long as the star's main-sequence phase
It lasts forever once formed

items.explain: Planetary nebulae are relatively short-lived, perhaps a few tens of millennia, compared to considerably longer phases of stellar evolution.

items.prompt: How might planetary nebulae affect the mix of elements in the Milky Way over time?

options.label: They pull elements out of space into stars
They destroy the elements stars made
They return elements made inside stars to space
They have no effect on the galaxy

items.explain: Planetary nebulae probably play a crucial role in the galaxy's chemical evolution by expelling elements into the interstellar medium from the stars where those elements were created.

items.prompt: In 1864 Huggins saw a bright line in a nebula's spectrum that matched no known element, and some proposed a new element. What was it?

options.label: A real new element that was later isolated on Earth
Familiar elements shining in extremely thin gas
A line caused by the glass of his prism
Helium, which was found in the Sun in 1868

items.explain: Nitrogen and oxygen ions in extremely low-density gas give rise to the line, called a forbidden line; 'nebulium' was never isolated on Earth.

items.prompt: Early observers saw round, planet-like shells. What did Hubble images from the 1990s show about their real shapes?

options.label: Most are not spherically symmetric
Nearly all are perfect spheres
All have exactly the same shape
Their shapes are fully explained by one cause

items.explain: Many have extremely complex and varied shapes; only about one-fifth are roughly spherical, and what produces the variety is not yet well understood.
